## 1. What you'll build, and why

Some redundancy only becomes visible at the very end. The SIL-level optimizer (Phase 4) saw values
and basic blocks; it could not see that, after register allocation, a value gets *stored to a slot
and loaded straight back into the same register*, or that the same slot is *loaded twice* in a row.
Those wastes exist only as concrete register/memory traffic in the final instruction stream — and
the pass that cleans them is the **peephole**: a small window sliding over the machine code,
rewriting obviously-wasteful patterns.

The headline rewrite turns a **redundant memory load into a register move**. A `ldr` reaches into
the data cache; a `mov` between registers is often eliminated entirely by the CPU's register
renamer (zero latency, zero execution ports). So replacing reloads with moves is a real, if modest,
improvement — and it's the canonical example of "local cleanup after register allocation."

- **You implement:** `rewrite_block` — the within-block local redundant-load elimination: track
  which register holds each slot, forward reloads to moves, and invalidate the bookkeeping on
  clobbers.
- **Outcome:** peephole-optimized code matches `swiftc`; on straight-line code the memory-load count
  drops (e.g. 18 → 11).

> **What's a peephole optimizer?** A pass that looks at a *small window* of consecutive instructions
> and replaces it with a cheaper equivalent — `mov x, x` → nothing, `mul x, x, #2` → `lsl x, x, #1`,
> a store-then-reload → a move. It's "peephole" because it sees only a keyhole's worth of code at a
> time. Simple, local, and exactly the right tool for redundancy the global passes can't express.

## 2. Concepts in depth

### Local redundant-load elimination

![The peephole, within a basic block: keep a slot→register table; when a slot is loaded whose value is already in a register, forward the reload to a `mov` (or drop it if the same register holds it). Invalidate the table when a tracked register is overwritten or a call clobbers state, and reset it at each block boundary. Honest note: this removes LOCAL redundancy; the variable-reloaded-every-block cost is CROSS-block and needs mem2reg, and scheduling is ~free on out-of-order cores.](figs/peephole.png)

The core idea is a tiny dataflow within one basic block. Keep a table `held : slot → register` that
answers "which register currently holds the value at this stack slot?" Then walk the block:

- **`str rs, [b,o]`** — the store stays (memory must actually be written), but now slot `(b,o)` is
  held by `rs`. (A store writes *memory*, not a register, and distinct stack slots don't alias, so
  nothing is invalidated.)
- **`ldr rd, [b,o]`** — if the table says `(b,o)` is in `rsrc`:
  - `rsrc = rd`? The value is *already in `rd`* — **drop the load**.
  - otherwise — replace the load with **`mov rd, rsrc`**: a register copy beats a memory access.
  - either way, after the load, `rd` holds `(b,o)`, so update the table.
- **`mov rd, rd`** — a move to self does nothing; **drop it**.
- **anything else** — it may *overwrite* registers. Any slot whose holder was just overwritten is
  now stale, so **invalidate** it. A `bl` (call) clobbers broadly, so clear the table.

### The IR you rewrite

Nothing is new here — no syntax, no SIL, not even a new ARM64 instruction. A peephole is a
function from an instruction stream to an instruction stream, and the only thing worth recalling
is which forms it has to recognize and what a "block" means to it (EBNF: `[ x ]` optional,
`{ x }` zero-or-more, `|` alternatives, quoted terminals):

```
block      ::= [ label ] { plain-instr } [ terminator ]
terminator ::= "B" | "Bcond" | "Bl" | "Ret" | "Brk"     (* also ENDS a block *)
matched    ::= "Str" reg base off        (* records: this slot is now in this register *)
             | "Ldr" reg base off        (* the rewrite candidate *)
             | "Mov" reg reg             (* the move-to-self case *)
other      ::= any instr                 (* may write registers: invalidate, never rewrite *)
```

The registers in the stream are all physical by now — this pass runs *after* allocation, which is
the point: the redundancy it removes is created by the spill rewrite and by the memory-based
lowering, and neither is visible before that. Two given helpers do all the plumbing:

| helper | what it gives you |
|---|---|
| `Arm64.reads_writes i` | the registers `i` reads and the ones it writes (`snd` is what to kill) |
| `Peephole.kill_reg held r` | forget every slot whose current holder is `r` |
| `Peephole.blocks_of instrs` | split the flat stream at labels and after terminators |

### Why invalidation is the whole game

The rewrites are easy; *correctness* is the table's invalidation. If a register that the table
thinks holds a slot's value gets overwritten, and you forward a later load to it anyway, you've
miscompiled. So every instruction that writes a register kills that register's entries; a call
clears everything; and the table **resets at each basic-block boundary** (control flow can merge
from elsewhere, where the table wouldn't hold). The alcotests check exactly these: a clobber
between the store and the reload keeps the reload a *load*, and there's no forwarding across a label.

### Running to a fixpoint

One rewrite can expose another (dropping a load may make the next instruction's pattern match), so
the pass iterates the per-block rewrite until nothing changes. The block splitting and the fixpoint
driver are given; you write the per-block rewrite.

### The honest part: which redundancy does this remove?

This is the lesson worth more than the code. Measure a hot loop like `collatz`: the peephole removes
*almost nothing* (one adjacent pair). Measure straight-line code that reuses variables: it removes a
lot (loads 18 → 11). The difference is **where the redundancy lives**:

- **Local (within a block):** a value reused several times in one straight-line stretch reloads the
  same slot repeatedly. The peephole forwards those to moves. ✔ This is what we remove.
- **Structural (across blocks):** because we lower the **memory-based** `-Onone` SIL, every variable
  lives in `alloc_stack`, so the *top of every basic block reloads it*. That redundancy spans block
  boundaries — the peephole's table resets there and can't touch it. Removing it needs **mem2reg /
  SSA promotion** (concept 34's exercise), which lifts variables into registers in the first place.

So the peephole's *runtime* win is small on our backend, and we report that honestly. The instruction
selection / register allocation we built earlier are the big levers; the peephole is the final
polish, and knowing it's *polish* — not the structural fix — is the point.

### Instruction scheduling, and why it's ~free here

The plan pairs peephole with **instruction scheduling**: reordering independent instructions to keep
the pipeline busy (e.g. issue a load several instructions before its result is needed, hiding its
latency). On an *in-order* core that's a real win. On Apple Silicon — a wide, deep **out-of-order**
core — the hardware reorders instructions itself within a large window, so a software scheduler's
benefit is close to nil. We keep the scheduler as the identity and say so. The honest hierarchy on
modern hardware: **fewer instructions (peephole) > reordered instructions (scheduling)**; a real
dependence-DAG list scheduler is the exercise, valuable mainly as a lesson about in-order targets.

> Oracle: LLVM's `MachineCSE`/`MachineSink`/peephole passes (the local cleanup) and its
> `PostRAScheduler` / `MachineScheduler` (the reordering). On `arm64-apple`, the scheduler's model
> reflects the core; we just acknowledge the OoO reality.

## 3. Build it, step by step

One hole, `rewrite_block` in `peephole.ml`, and it is a single walk over one block carrying the
`held : slot → register` table. §2 states the four rules the walk has to implement; the work is
turning them into a loop that keeps the table TRUE at every step.

Two things to get right, and they are the two the tests separate:

1. **The rewrites.** A `ldr` of a slot the table already accounts for is either a `mov` or
   nothing at all — decide which by looking at where the value already is. A store teaches the
   table something; a load teaches it something too, and forgetting that is the usual reason a
   second reload survives.
2. **The invalidation.** Every instruction that WRITES a register makes some entries false, and
   the general case is not `Ldr`/`Str`/`Mov` — it is everything else, which is why
   `Arm64.reads_writes` is given. A call is the broad case. Set `changed` whenever you actually
   rewrite something, or the fixpoint stops early.

Given: `mem_key`, `kill_reg`, `blocks_of`, the fixpoint driver `peephole`, the (identity)
scheduler, and the driver wiring (`--no-peephole` turns the pass off, which is how the tests
compare). Reference: `solution/peephole.ml`. Run with
`make lab C=phase8-arm64-backend/36-peephole-sched`.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase8-arm64-backend/36-peephole-sched
```

The hole is one function with two halves — what it rewrites and what it must refuse to rewrite —
so there is one cram file for each.

- **`tests/peephole-forward.t`** is the rewriting half: a straight-line program's `ldr` count
  falling (18 → 11), a store-then-reload-the-same-register pair losing its load outright, and
  reloads into other registers turning into the `mov`s that replace them. Every case ends by
  running the program against `swiftc` *and* against the `--no-peephole` backend.
- **`tests/peephole-invalidate.t`** is the refusing half, and it is where the pass is actually
  hard: a clobbered holder, a `bl`, and a loop header reached from two edges. It closes with the
  honest measurement — the pass trims what it can see inside the loop body, but the reloads that
  open each iteration survive, because that redundancy is cross-block and belongs to mem2reg.
- **`tests/oracle.t`** asks swiftc every run: 32 programs (concept 35's corpus), each built by
  `swiftc -Onone`, by Backend A, and by Backend B **both ways** — with the pass and with
  `--no-peephole` — then run and required byte-identical. The `--no-peephole` build is the
  control: an optimization is only correct if the program means the same thing without it, and a
  peephole that forwards a stale register produces a plausible wrong number, not a crash.
- **`tests/test_peephole.ml`** works on hand-built instruction streams, where a rule can be
  stated exactly: three rewrite shapes (drop, forward-to-`mov`, `mov`-to-self) and four soundness
  guards (a clobbered holder keeps the load, a `bl` resets the table, a store to an *unrelated*
  slot does not invalidate, and nothing forwards across a label), plus the load count of a real
  program falling.

Reading the report: the hole is one function, so both cram files and the alcotest suite go from
`TODO … not started` to green together. `oracle.t` shows `FAIL` rather than `TODO`, because its
front-end case passes before you write a line.

## 5. Benchmark it

Report it honestly. On `collatz` (cross-block-dominated), peephole removes ~one instruction and
runtime is flat. On straight-line, variable-reuse code, it cuts memory loads ~40% (most becoming
register moves). The runtime delta on an out-of-order core is small either way — the lesson is that
the *measurable* effect is fewer memory accesses, and the *structural* win (variables in registers)
belongs to mem2reg, not here.

## 6. Exercises

1. **Strength reduction.** `mul x, x, #2ⁿ` → `lsl x, x, #n`; `sdiv x, x, #2ⁿ` of a known-positive
   value → an arithmetic shift. Requires the constant to be visible (track `mov rk, #imm`).
2. **Immediate folding.** `mov rk, #c; add rd, ra, rk` → `add rd, ra, #c` when `c` fits the 12-bit
   immediate — removes a register and an instruction.
3. **Dead-store elimination.** A `str rs, [slot]` whose slot is overwritten by another store before
   any load (within the block) is dead — drop it. The dual of redundant-load elimination.
4. **Branch peepholes.** `b.cond L; b M; L:` → `b.!cond M` (fall through to `L`); collapse a `b` to
   the very next label; remove unreachable code after an unconditional `b`/`ret`.
5. **A real list scheduler.** Build the dependence DAG of a block (RAW/WAR/WAW edges), and
   list-schedule it to separate producers from consumers by the instruction's latency. Measure on an
   in-order target (e.g. via a simulator) — the case where it actually pays.

## 7. Recap & what's next

The peephole is the final-polish pass: within a basic block, forward a redundant memory load to a
register move (and drop the truly-dead), with careful invalidation for soundness. It removes *local*
redundancy honestly and modestly; the *structural* redundancy (variables in memory, reloaded every
block) is mem2reg's job, and scheduling is ~free on out-of-order cores. Matching the pass to the
redundancy is the lesson.

Next, **37-debug-info** — thread source locations end-to-end, emit a DWARF-lite line table, and step
through a `swiftml`-built binary in `lldb` — to reach **M8-core** (the native backend, complete and
debuggable).

## 8. Appendix — full solution

```ocaml
let rewrite_block (changed : bool ref) (instrs : Arm64.instr list) : Arm64.instr list =
  let held : (Arm64.reg * int, Arm64.reg) Hashtbl.t = Hashtbl.create 16 in
  let out = ref [] in
  let emit i = out := i :: !out in
  List.iter
    (fun (i : Arm64.instr) ->
      match i with
      | Arm64.Str (rs, b, o) -> emit i; Hashtbl.replace held (mem_key b o) rs
      | Arm64.Ldr (rd, b, o) -> (
          (match Hashtbl.find_opt held (mem_key b o) with
          | Some rsrc when rsrc = rd -> changed := true                          (* drop *)
          | Some rsrc -> changed := true; kill_reg held rd; emit (Arm64.Mov (rd, Arm64.R rsrc))
          | None -> kill_reg held rd; emit i);
          Hashtbl.replace held (mem_key b o) rd)
      | Arm64.Mov (rd, Arm64.R rs) when rd = rs -> changed := true               (* mov self *)
      | other ->
          let _, writes = Arm64.reads_writes other in
          List.iter (kill_reg held) writes;
          (match other with Arm64.Bl _ -> Hashtbl.reset held | _ -> ());
          emit other)
    instrs;
  List.rev !out
```

## 9. Exercise solutions

### 1 — strength reduction
Track `mov rk, #c` (a constant in a register). When you see `mul rd, ra, rk` with `c = 2ⁿ`, emit
`lsl rd, ra, #n`. A multiply is a few cycles; a shift is one. (Many compilers do this at the IR
level; doing it post-RA catches constants that survived to the machine code.)

### 2 — immediate folding
Same constant tracking: `mov rk, #c; add rd, ra, rk` → `add rd, ra, #c` when `0 ≤ c < 4096`. The
arithmetic instructions take a 12-bit immediate directly, so the materializing `mov` and the extra
register both disappear. Watch the range (and the optional shift-by-12).

### 3 — dead-store elimination
Within a block, if `str rs, [slot]` is followed (before any `ldr [slot]` or `bl`) by another `str
_, [slot]`, the first store is dead — its value is never observed. Track the last store per slot;
when a new store to the same slot arrives with no intervening read, delete the previous one.

### 4 — branch peepholes
`b.cond L; b M; L: …` inverts to `b.!cond M; L: …` (fall through to `L`), saving a branch. A `b` to
the immediately-following label is dead. Instructions after an unconditional `b`/`ret`, up to the
next label, are unreachable — delete them. These shrink the CFG's edges, the machine-code analogue
of concept 17's `simplify_cfg`.

### 5 — a real list scheduler
Per block: build a DAG with an edge from each instruction to the later instructions that depend on
it (read-after-write through registers/memory). Topologically list-schedule, at each step picking a
ready instruction whose inputs were produced longest ago (greedily hiding latency). It helps on
in-order cores (Cortex-A53, many embedded targets); on Apple's OoO cores, measuring it is the lesson
in why it's ~free there.
```
